verdicts.reason: X measures explicit praise/flattery of the agency while Y measures relational familiarity cues such as named officials and prior dealings, and a comment can be warmly complimentary with no relationship or coldly transactional with a long relationship.
Both fire on the same trigger set of quantified organizational scale (market share, employee counts, membership rolls), so scores would be essentially interchangeable.
Both score the writer's place-plus-tenure standing claim as a credibility device and would rank comments almost identically, differing only in midpoint anchoring.

X requires substantive precision in mapping text to CFR/statutory provisions while Y scores legal register and memo formatting, so a polished counsel-style letter voicing only broad opposition scores high on Y and zero on X.

X requires an ongoing formal or informal history with the agency, whereas Y also fires on shallow cues like naming an official or thanking staff for coordination, which a first-time commenter can supply.
Citing CFR parts and sections is a citation-practice measure while exceeding statutory authority is a specific legal argument, and either can appear without the other.
Both require self-derived numeric compliance-cost figures with a stated basis and score zero absent numbers.

X credits any personal or sectoral positioning including bare job title or corporate role, while Y requires tenure, residency, or place/trade identity, so an officer identifying only by corporate title scores high on X and low on Y.

X covers the whole class of procedural asks including re-noticing, earlier publication, and status tracking, whereas Y is confined to delay or extension requests, so a non-delay procedural ask scores high on X and zero on Y.

X requires description of an internal drafting or working-group process, while Y measures breadth of represented organizations, so a long multi-signatory coalition letter scores high on Y with no internal-process language.
Both reward advertisement of institutional scale credentials and would fire together on essentially the same self-descriptive passages.

Y adds a proportionality requirement, explicitly scoring zero for a brief one-line identification, whereas X scores 10 for any explicit itemization of scale, so a one-sentence membership figure diverges sharply.
Both identify mass-campaign form text from its formulaic, duplicated, non-individualized wording and score bespoke prose at zero.

Y requires expert authority credentials such as senior title, licensing, or specialized expertise, while X credits ordinary local identity or occupational role, so a self-identified local resident and farmer scores high on X and low on Y.
X requires multiple lengthy paragraphs of boilerplate (a density measure), while Y fires on any formulaic slogan or stock demand, so a short three-line form letter scores 10 on Y and low on X.

X scores professional rulemaking register and counsel-style drafting while Y scores precise mapping to provisions and explicitly zeroes broad approval or opposition, so a polished but non-specific letter splits the two.
Both score explicit disclosure of a prior or ongoing relationship with the agency using nearly identical exemplars (prior permits, recurring meetings, previous dealings).

X requires a case-law citation apparatus or a counsel letterhead/signature block, while Y fires on generic legal-memo formatting and phrases like Respectfully submitted that appear in comments with no case law at all.
X requires described prior dealings with the agency, whereas Y also counts naming an official or thanking staff for coordination, cues a first-time commenter can display without any relationship.
Boilerplate campaign density measures unoriginal advocacy prose while authority stacking measures piled statutes, cases, and studies, and these typically appear in opposite kinds of comments.
Both score the same artifact set of portal/email headers, attachment placeholders, filenames, OCR defects, and duplicated cover text.

The scales run in opposite directions (X rewards plain conversational register, Y rewards legalese) and X also penalizes dense non-legal technical prose that Y would score low, so the two are anti-correlated rather than interchangeable.
Both score whether a concrete, implementable regulatory alternative is described and give zero when the comment merely objects.
Both measure the comment's claim to speak for a large named multi-organization coalition or consensus and score individual submissions at zero.

Authority stacking rewards volume of citations without proportionate explanation while regulatory-lawyer fluency rewards precise provision-level mapping, so a citation-dense but imprecise comment scores high on X and low on Y.
First-hand operational experience is a content/evidence measure while intensity of expressed feeling is an affect measure, and either can occur without the other.
Both reward the same self-advertised institutional scale credentials (size, membership, market share, reach) and would produce closely tracking scores.

X credits polished administrative rulemaking competence including structured regulatory edits in plain professional prose, while Y requires legal-memo formatting, reporters, or dense legalese, so a trade-association policy letter scores high on X and low on Y.
